Do not assume an embolic mechanism and miss the critical right ICA stenosis: the watershed pattern and blood-pressure-dependent fluctuations point to a hemodynamic mechanism.
Do not label the stuttering course as TIA without neuroimaging: DWI-positive watershed lesions are completed infarction, not transient ischemia.
Do not delay vascular imaging of the carotid arteries: a symptomatic severe ICA stenosis needs revascularization within 2 weeks.

required_recommendations: Establish last known well (about 2 hours before arrival: he returned fully to baseline after each earlier episode, so the stuttering course does not move it) and the NIHSS (6: gaze 1, left arm 2, left leg 2, sensory 1).
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision.
Obtain CTA of the head and neck urgently to identify the symptomatic severe right ICA stenosis and to exclude a large vessel occlusion.

IV thrombolysis: give, once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (about 2 hours from last known well; disabling left hemiparesis; CT without hemorrhage; glucose 108 mg/dL, platelets 244, INR 1.0; aspirin use and a colonoscopy 5 days ago without polypectomy or bleeding are not contraindications). Thrombectomy: not indicated (no large vessel occlusion; the right ICA is severely stenosed but patent and the intracranial arteries are open).

Lower blood pressure (192/106 mmHg) cautiously to just below 185/110 mmHg with small titrated doses of IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; avoid overshoot, because his deficit worsened when systolic pressure fell to 146 mmHg.
Give alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) with a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.
Watch for orolingual angioedema during and after the thrombolytic infusion: he takes lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Recognize the right internal watershed (rosary-bead) DWI pattern, the proximal-predominant weakness and the blood-pressure-dependent fluctuation as a hemodynamic (low-flow) mechanism from the right ICA stenosis rather than a cortical territorial embolus.

Identify the hemodynamic trigger: the procedural hypotension (72/44 mmHg) during colonoscopy and the reduced oral intake since, superimposed on the 85-90% right ICA stenosis. Withholding his antihypertensives around the procedure is not a hypotensive trigger.

Avoid hypotension and volume depletion until the stenosis is treated: give isotonic fluids (BUN 22 mg/dL after poor intake), do not restart lisinopril and amlodipine in the first 48 to 72 hours, then resume them gradually; set the long-term target below 130/80 mmHg once the stenosis is revascularized.

After imaging at 24 hours excludes hemorrhage, start antiplatelet therapy for the large-artery mechanism: continue aspirin and add clopidogrel 75 mg daily as short-term dual therapy while awaiting revascularization, then a single agent, with the regimen agreed with the vascular surgeon (NIHSS 6 is outside the CHANCE/POINT minor-stroke range).
Replace omeprazole with pantoprazole while he takes clopidogrel: omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and reduces clopidogrel activation.

Refer for right carotid revascularization (endarterectomy, or stenting if surgical risk is high) between 2 days and 2 weeks after the stroke: a symptomatic 70-99% stenosis is a class I indication when perioperative risk is below 6% (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention). Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg (LDL 138 mg/dL on 40 mg) and add ezetimibe if LDL stays at or above 70 mg/dL (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention).

key_clinical_evidence: The right internal (deep) watershed pattern, multiple small DWI-positive foci in a rosary-bead distribution along the corona radiata and centrum semiovale, is the neuroimaging signature of hemodynamic (low-flow) ischemia rather than cortical territorial embolism.
The proximal-predominant left hemiparesis (shoulder and hip weaker than hand and foot) is the clinical correlate of the borderzone infarction.
NIHSS is 6 (gaze 1, left arm 2, left leg 2, sensory 1); limb ataxia is 0 because the imprecision is in proportion to weakness, and there is no neglect or extinction.

Critical right ICA stenosis (85-90%) reduces perfusion reserve; the procedural hypotension (nadir 72/44 mmHg) during colonoscopy and poor oral intake since dropped distal perfusion below the autoregulatory threshold. Withholding antihypertensives around the procedure is not a hypotensive trigger.

The stuttering course with blood-pressure-dependent fluctuation is the key red herring: it suggests recurrent TIA or seizure, but it is characteristic of a flow-dependent mechanism. Because he returned fully to baseline after each earlier episode, last known well is about 2 hours before arrival.

IV thrombolysis is given once blood pressure is brought just below 185/110 mmHg: about 2 hours from last known well, disabling deficit, no hemorrhage, normal glucose, platelets and INR; a colonoscopy without polypectomy or bleeding is not a contraindication. No thrombectomy: no large vessel occlusion.

Blood pressure lowering is limited to what thrombolysis requires and must avoid overshoot: his deficit worsened at 146/82 mmHg because the borderzone depends on perfusion pressure through the stenosis.

CTA is the load-bearing study: it shows the symptomatic 85-90% right ICA stenosis with irregular plaque, the therapeutic target for revascularization between 2 days and 2 weeks (AHA/ASA 2021); emergent endarterectomy within 48 hours is not beneficial (AHA/ASA 2026 §4.12).
No atrial fibrillation on Holter and a normal echo with normal left atrial size make a cardioembolic mechanism unlikely, consistent with large-artery atherosclerosis (TOAST).
He takes lisinopril (angioedema risk with the thrombolytic) and omeprazole (reduces clopidogrel activation; switch to pantoprazole).
Only glucose had to be known before thrombolysis here (no anticoagulant, no suspected coagulopathy); ECG and troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA does not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ronald Hadley is a 70-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, active smoking, and peripheral arterial disease who is brought to the emergency department by his wife with a 5-day history of recurring left-sided arm and leg weakness, now present continuously for approximately 2 hours. The patient underwent an elective screening colonoscopy 5 days ago and tolerated the procedure without obvious complications, though the endoscopy team recorded a blood pressure nadir of 72/44 mmHg lasting approximately 4 minutes during the procedure. No polyps were removed, and he has had no rectal bleeding since. He was discharged home the same day and has eaten and drunk less than usual since. Beginning the evening of the colonoscopy, he experienced episodes of heaviness and clumsiness involving his left arm and leg, each lasting between 20 and 90 minutes and resolving completely; between episodes he walked and used his arm normally. His wife noticed that the left arm weakness seemed most pronounced in the shoulder and upper arm, with his grip remaining relatively preserved; she compared it to 'not being able to lift his arm.' Over the following days he had four further similar episodes. He and his wife initially attributed these events to post-procedural fatigue or 'bad circulation.' On the day of presentation he was at his baseline until approximately 2 hours before arrival, when he developed persistent left arm and leg weakness that did not resolve. His wife observed that when he sat upright rapidly after lying down, the weakness appeared to transiently worsen. He denies headache at symptom onset, visual changes, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria (speech has been normal throughout), nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, or chest pain. He has no known history of atrial fibrillation. He reports that he did not take his antihypertensive medications on the morning of the colonoscopy as instructed by the gastroenterology team, and again did not take them the morning after the procedure because he 'felt off.' There was no witnessed seizure. Last known neurologically intact time is approximately 2 hours prior to arrival. In the emergency department, blood pressure was 188/102 mmHg on arrival and 192/106 mmHg 15 minutes later. A fall to 146/82 mmHg after a small dose of opioid analgesia for a mild headache was followed by worsening of left arm heaviness, which partially improved as the blood pressure rose again.

neurological_exam.additional: NIHSS score: 6 (gaze 1, left arm 2, left leg 2, sensory 1). Proximal-predominant left hemiparesis pattern noted. No meningismus. Blood pressure 188/102 mmHg on arrival; repeat measurement at 15 minutes 192/106 mmHg. During a transient BP drop to 146/82 mmHg after opioid analgesia for a headache, patient reported worsening of left arm heaviness, which partially recovered as BP rose again.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact on right. Left finger-to-nose slightly imprecise due to proximal arm weakness. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light. Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Partial gaze preference to the right, overcome on command; full range of conjugate eye movements on examination. No facial asymmetry at rest or with voluntary movement. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline. Right carotid bruit audible on auscultation.
neurological_exam.gait: Deferred in the acute setting due to left leg proximal weakness. Patient assisted to stand; leans leftward and unable to bear full weight on left.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal prosody, no aphasia, no paraphasias. Comprehension intact to multi-step commands. No neglect of left-sided stimuli. Able to name objects without hesitation. Serial sevens with 1 error in 5.
neurological_exam.motor: Left upper extremity: 3/5 proximal deltoid and shoulder abduction, 3/5 elbow flexion, 4/5 grip strength; proximal weakness disproportionate to distal. Left lower extremity: 3/5 hip flexion, 3+/5 knee extension, 4+/5 ankle dorsiflexion; proximal predominance. Right upper and lower extremities: 5/5 throughout. On NIHSS testing the left arm cannot hold 90 degrees and drifts down to the bed within 10 seconds, and the left leg falls to the bed within 5 seconds, both with some effort against gravity. No fasciculations. Normal bulk bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Left biceps 3+, triceps 3+, brachioradialis 2+, patellar 3+, Achilles 2+. Right upper and lower extremities: all 2+ and symmetric. Left plantar response upgoing (Babinski sign). Right plantar response flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild diminution of pinprick over the left arm and leg without a clear cortical level. Proprioception intact at toes bilaterally. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
